prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and its development into long-acting incretin therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: Round 1 showed that all six of us agree on the science. The GLP-1 chain runs from proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, through the active truncated peptide and receptor biology, to protracted-action agonists. Independent replication and large randomized outcome trials in diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal disease leave no question of maturity. The only open matter is what the third place honours. I keep Drucker and Holst for physiology and receptor and tissue biology. I keep Knudsen because the physiology only became medicine through stable, albumin-binding acylated analogues, and a prize in this category that states the arc from hormone to drug is consistent with its mandate. I have not changed my preferred configuration. I have, however, sharpened the reason. This is a considered judgment about what the citation should say and not a claim that Mojsov's contribution is small.
statement.case_against: The strongest argument against my trio is the one made by four colleagues. The Nobel tradition rewards the discovery that opened a field, identification of the active peptide is upstream of every analogue, and Knudsen's work was done by an industrial team that optimised known pharmacology. I cannot dismiss that. My trio also leaves Mojsov out under the three-person cap, which risks resolving a disputed credit by omission, and Habener sits outside the credited names in any configuration. If the committee weighs the discovery-side reading more heavily, the Mojsov trio is a legitimate and coherent prize, and I would not regard it as a mistake. My own reservation is that a discovery-only citation honours the hormone but not the molecules that reached patients, and that Knudsen's individual contribution is more separable within a company team than the file lets me state with confidence.

responses.point: Prefers Mojsov to Knudsen because active-peptide identification is upstream of every analogue, calls Knudsen's work optimisation of known pharmacology by an industrial team, and says the Mojsov dispute alone should not remove her because it would also unsettle Holst and Drucker.
responses.response: Your last point is right, and I withdraw any implication that the dispute alone justifies omitting Mojsov. My case for Knudsen rests on the contribution, not on the cap. I do not accept that acylation was optimisation. Attaching a fatty acid so that the peptide binds albumin and escapes DPP-4 and renal clearance is a design principle. It is not a routine screen, and it made once-daily and then once-weekly dosing possible. You are right that picking among liraglutide, semaglutide and the dual agonists is hard, and that favours crediting the design principle through one named person and not an individual product. Where we differ is the weight of upstream identification against that principle. Since you want Mojsov's weight tested, I should say that I cannot test it from the file. I will not rest my position on a deciding factor I cannot verify.

responses.point: Would not object strongly to the Knudsen trio if Mojsov's priority is judged too uncertain, calls it a close call, and prefers to keep industrial drug optimisation separate from the discovery credit.
responses.response: I take the close call at face value, and it is how I see it too. I accept that the physiology credit is thinner without Mojsov. My answer is the citation wording. It names the physiology of GLP-1 and the development of long-acting therapies, so the identification of the active form is covered by Holst and Drucker's work on the truncated peptide's action, without crediting a priority claim I cannot settle. If the committee believes that stretches Holst's and Drucker's work too far, I would accept your concern as decisive for that reading. I would still not call the drug-design step separable from the prize case, because without it the physiology reaches patients as a short-lived peptide.

responses.point: Prefers Mojsov as the third name but would not block a Knudsen variant, and argues that dropping Mojsov because of the cap resolves a disputed credit by omission, not by evidence.
responses.response: Your objection that the cap resolves a disputed credit by omission is fair, and I considered it again. The difficulty is symmetric, because any trio resolves the Mojsov-Knudsen choice by omission. The question is which omission is more defensible if we have to explain it. I think leaving out an industrial scientist whose work produced the usable drug is harder to justify than leaving out a contributor whose priority is disputed. I recognise that this judgment depends on the weight I give to translation, and I know you weigh it differently. I appreciate that you would not block my trio. I would say the same of yours.

responses.point: Calls long-acting pharmacology an engineering step that follows the discovery, keeps Mojsov for peptide identification and would revisit if her contribution proves less decisive.
responses.response: I do not think we disagree on the facts, only on whether the engineering step is part of the discovery. I would call it part of it in this case. Native GLP-1 has a half-life of minutes and would not have become a therapy without a molecular solution to that problem, so the biology reached patients through that solution. You said you would revisit if Mojsov's contribution proves less decisive. I will make a reciprocal statement. If the committee can establish that Knudsen's design work cannot be separated from a company programme, I would have a reason to move to the Mojsov trio, and I would then accept a citation narrowed to physiology and the identification of the active peptide.

responses.point: Prefers Drucker, Holst and Knudsen but says she could move to a Mojsov trio if the citation were narrowed to physiology and peptide identification, and keeps B021 as first alternative with Rosenberg as the conceptual base.
responses.response: We hold the same trio and I will not pretend that gives it extra weight. I also note that your readiness to move to Mojsov under a narrower citation shows how close the choice is. On B021, I still prefer a June and Sadelain pair. Adoptive transfer is the conceptual base, but Rosenberg's TIL work is a distinct discovery and the Eshhar gap makes a three-name credit hard to explain. That is why I list it second among alternatives behind B006. I disclosed that we have co-authored work, and it does not affect my view of the shortlist.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a discovery-side GLP-1 prize or a discovery-to-medicine prize, which is the real decision behind the Mojsov and Knudsen choice.
Whether Mojsov's weight relative to Habener can be established, because I cannot settle it from the file and I do not rely on recollection of the historical record.
Whether Knudsen's individual contribution can be separated from a company programme with enough confidence to credit one name.
Whether a prize that fits the three-person cap but credits neither side of the Mojsov and Knudsen dispute could be acceptable, because B006 would be the cleaner but less consequential alternative.
statement.conflict_note: No documented involvement with any credited name on the shortlist. My profile records eight co-authored works with fellow committee member Rickard Sandberg and co-authorship of the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper in Science. Neither involves a shortlisted candidate and I infer no personal tie. No recusal is requested.
